lines.text:
Capturing the Moment — Inside a Photography Studio

Ahmed is a professional photographer. Every morning, he arrives at his photography studio, opens his camera bag, and prepares for the day. His main camera is a DSLR — a professional camera with interchangeable lenses. He also has a mirrorless camera, which is smaller and lighter.

The studio is set up for portrait photography. A backdrop — a large sheet of coloured paper — hangs from a frame at the back. Today it is white. A posing stool sits in the centre for the subject. On the props table, there are sunglasses, hats, and books that clients can hold. A wardrobe rack holds clothes for fashion shoots. A makeup station with a mirror and lights stands in the corner.

Lighting is the most important part of studio photography. A softbox creates soft, even light. An umbrella light bounces the flash off a white surface to reduce harsh shadows. A ring light creates a circular glow around the subject's face — popular for beauty photography. A reflector — a white or gold disc — bounces light into dark areas. A diffuser softens bright light. Each light sits on a light stand. A strobe flashes brightly for a fraction of a second. A gel filter changes the colour of the light. Continuous lights stay on all the time and are used for video.

Ahmed picks up his camera. He looks through the viewfinder and adjusts the focus ring on his telephoto lens until the subject is sharp. For wider shots, he changes to a wide-angle lens. The lens cap protects the glass when the lens is not in use. A lens hood blocks unwanted light. He presses the shutter button. The camera clicks. The image is saved on a memory card inside the camera. The battery must be fully charged — Ahmed always carries a spare.

A tripod keeps the camera steady for slow shutter speeds. A monopod offers support with more mobility. A camera strap keeps the camera safe around his neck. Clamps, sandbags, and gaffer tape hold equipment in place. An extension cord reaches the far side of the studio.

After the shoot, Ahmed connects his camera to a computer monitor and opens the editing software. He adjusts the brightness, contrast, and colour using a colour wheel. A histogram shows the distribution of light and dark tones. He uses the crop tool to improve composition, the brush tool for touch-ups, and layers to make non-destructive changes. A filter or preset can change the mood of the entire image with one click.

The hot shoe on top of the camera holds an external flash. The LCD screen on the back shows a preview. The dial on top controls the camera's settings — shutter speed, aperture, and ISO. The image sensor inside the camera captures the light and creates the photograph.

Ahmed says: 'A camera is just a tool. The photographer's eye — knowing what to include and what to leave out — that's what makes a great photograph.'

lines.text: Can you set up the light stand on the left and attach the softbox? I want soft, even light on the backdrop.

lines.text: ❌ "She made a beautiful photo of the sunset yesterday."
lines.name: ❌ "She made a beautiful photo of the sunset yesterday."

lines.text: ✅ "She took a beautiful photo of the sunset yesterday."
lines.name: ✅ "She took a beautiful photo of the sunset yesterday."

lines.text: We 'take' a photo — not 'make' a photo. 'Take a photo/picture/selfie/screenshot.' 'Make' is used for creating things from raw materials: 'make a cake', 'make a film.' But photos are 'taken' — the camera captures what already exists.

lines.text: ❌ "I need a new equipment for my studio."
lines.name: ❌ "I need a new equipment for my studio."

lines.text: ✅ "I need new equipment for my studio." / "I need a new piece of equipment."
lines.name: ✅ "I need new equipment for my studio." / "I need a new piece of equipment."

lines.text: 'Equipment' is uncountable — no 'a' and no plural. 'I need new equipment.' 'A piece of equipment.' Not: 'an equipment' or 'equipments.' Similar uncountable nouns: 'furniture', 'luggage', 'advice', 'information.'

lines.text: ❌ "The photographer adjusted the light so that the photo looks good."
lines.name: ❌ "The photographer adjusted the light so that the photo looks good."

lines.text: ✅ "The photographer adjusted the light so that the photo would look good."
lines.name: ✅ "The photographer adjusted the light so that the photo would look good."

lines.text: After a past tense main verb ('adjusted'), the subordinate clause uses past or conditional forms: 'so that the photo would look good.' This is called 'backshift' or sequence of tenses. 'She moved the reflector so that the light would be softer.'

lines.text: ❌ "He has a very expensive camera. He must to be a professional."
lines.name: ❌ "He has a very expensive camera. He must to be a professional."

lines.text: ✅ "He has a very expensive camera. He must be a professional."
lines.name: ✅ "He has a very expensive camera. He must be a professional."

lines.text: Modal verbs (must, can, should, will, may) take a bare infinitive — no 'to.' 'He must be a professional.' 'She can take great photos.' Never 'must to be' or 'can to do.'

lines.text: ❌ "I'm used to take photos with my phone, not with a professional camera."
lines.name: ❌ "I'm used to take photos with my phone, not with a professional camera."

lines.text: ✅ "I'm used to taking photos with my phone, not with a professional camera."
lines.name: ✅ "I'm used to taking photos with my phone, not with a professional camera."

lines.text: 'Be used to + -ing' = be accustomed to: 'I'm used to taking photos with my phone.' The 'to' is a preposition, not an infinitive marker. Compare: 'I used to take photos with film' (past habit, now stopped). These are different structures with different meanings.

lines.text: 'Photo' is the most common everyday word. 'Photograph' is more formal. 'Picture' is general and can mean a photo, painting, or drawing. 'Image' is used in digital/professional contexts. 'Snap' is informal British for a quick photo.

lines.text: UK passport photos have strict rules: white background, neutral expression, no glasses, face fully visible. They must be 35mm x 45mm. Photo booths and studios both offer passport photo services.

lines.text: 'Selfie' entered the Oxford English Dictionary in 2013. 'Selfie stick' is the extending pole used to take selfies. 'Photobomb' means appearing unexpectedly in someone's photo. These are common B1-B2 vocabulary items.

lines.text: In the UK, you can generally photograph in public places. However, photographing children (especially at schools) requires permission. 'Model release' is a signed form allowing use of someone's image commercially.

lines.text: 'Analogue' (British) / 'analog' (American) photography uses film. 'Digital' photography uses electronic sensors. 'Darkroom' is where film is developed. Many photography terms come from the film era: 'exposure', 'negative', 'develop'.
